title: Med Handoff Card
user: An adult child or home caregiver coordinating an older relative's changing medication schedule who needs an unambiguous, shareable record of what was taken, held, or newly prescribed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says an elderly family member frequently loses track of many medications and doctors lack a complete current-medication view; replies propose a time-of-day checklist and adherence packaging.
The requested tracker centers on medicine name, dosage, schedule, and an updatable list, confirming that a durable current regimen is a concrete user need.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–2026 requests; the caregiver case is high severity because an unclear dose state can cause a missed or duplicate dose.
current_workaround: Paper charts, a spreadsheet/Numbers checklist, pill boxes, text messages, or a pharmacy blister pack.
incumbents_and_gap: Medisafe and MyTherapy focus on individual reminders; Apple Health stores health records. The unresolved gap is a printable, caregiver-safe shift handoff that records exceptions and regimen changes without requiring every family member to create an account.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA with a large time-of-day dose board, taken/held/unknown states, a current-medication card, QR export, and a one-page handoff printout. Non-goals: drug-interaction advice, diagnosis, prescription refills, or emergency alerts.
success_measure: In a 30-day caregiver pilot, 80% of scheduled doses have a recorded state and a substitute caregiver can correctly state the current regimen from the generated handoff card.
monetization: one-time — this is safety-adjacent household recordkeeping where no-account ownership and offline use are more credible than a subscription.
constraints: Treat all data as sensitive health data; encrypt local export when the user chooses it; clear medical-disclaimer language; do not make clinical or interaction claims.
why_distinct: It is a caregiver handoff and exception log, not another reminder app or pill-dispenser marketplace.

title: Symptom Visit Brief
user: A person with intermittent or hard-to-explain symptoms who needs to turn brief daily observations into a factual timeline a clinician can review.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker describes five years of gut issues and normal tests across four doctors, contrasting that experience with the observability expected from work dashboards.
The health-diary request explicitly asks for symptom severity, history, filtering by illness, and severity color coding.

recurrence: Two independent health-tracking discussions in 2026; the pain persists across multiple appointments and makes appointments less productive.
current_workaround: Memory, phone notes, a spreadsheet, or a broad mood/health diary that does not produce a visit-ready summary.
incumbents_and_gap: Bearable, Guava, and Apple Health collect extensive data, but their dashboards can bury the short chronological story a clinician needs. A low-friction, exportable symptom narrative remains underserved.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first daily check-in with symptom, severity, duration, trigger/context, and optional photo; it renders a date-bounded one-page PDF/CSV visit brief with plain counts and trends. Non-goals: diagnosis, treatment recommendations, wearable ingestion, or provider portal integration.
success_measure: At least 60% of weekly active users export a visit brief before an appointment, and at least half report adding one detail they otherwise would have forgotten.
monetization: one-time — personal medical notes should not be held behind a recurring account fee.
constraints: Keep records on device by default; make exports explicit; avoid medical-device claims and any diagnostic scoring; accessible severity controls are required.
why_distinct: The product is a concise evidence packet for a real appointment, not an AI health coach or generic quantified-self dashboard.

title: Durable Set Log
user: A strength trainee using a phone during a workout who needs every completed set retained even if the PWA reloads, loses signal, or is evicted from memory.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A personal trainer asks whether the open-source workout platform will support workout sharing and integrations with Strava, Garmin Connect, HealthKit, Google Fit, and Coros.
The issue documents that optimistic workout updates are only in memory and that an iOS reload can silently drop queued sets; it asks for an IndexedDB write-ahead log and replay.

recurrence: Two fitness-tool communities identify workout logging/integration friction; silent loss is severe because progressive-overload history is the core record.
current_workaround: Notes, Google Keep, a paper notebook, or waiting for a cloud-backed fitness app to reconnect.
incumbents_and_gap: Hevy, Strong, and FitNotes provide full trackers, while social platforms emphasize sharing. The gap is a tiny offline-first set ledger whose failure mode is inspectable and recoverable.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA for reusable routines, one-tap set completion, edit-safe append-only local log, and CSV export/import. Non-goals: exercise video library, social feed, AI programming, nutrition tracking, or cloud accounts.
success_measure: Across 100 deliberate offline/reload tests, 100% of confirmed sets reappear after reopening; 50% of pilot users complete three workouts a week for four weeks.
monetization: one-time — reliability and data ownership are the value, not an ongoing coaching subscription.
constraints: Use IndexedDB with export/restore and conflict-free local identifiers; state clearly that this is not medical guidance; support large text and one-handed controls.
why_distinct: It narrows the product to durable workout capture and recovery rather than cloning a social fitness suite.

title: Flex Calorie Ledger
user: An adult trying to manage food intake around variable real activity who wants a simple private weekly ledger instead of a rigid daily target or an account-heavy diet platform.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The maker of a no-account diet app says existing apps use fixed calorie targets, do not flex with actual activity, are fiddly to log into, or require another account.
A disabled user asks for physical-symptom tracking because amnesia makes it difficult to explain flare-ups to doctors, illustrating the need for lightweight body context rather than isolated numbers.

recurrence: Two 2026 self-tracking requests emphasize low-friction, contextual personal records; rigid daily targets make adherence harder when activity and symptoms vary.
current_workaround: A fixed target in MyFitnessPal/Lose It!, notes, or mentally compensating on high- and low-activity days.
incumbents_and_gap: MyFitnessPal, Lose It!, Cronometer, and MacroFactor are comprehensive trackers, but they are often account-centric and food-database-heavy. The gap is an intentionally small, activity-aware weekly budget that accepts estimates and context.
smallest_useful_product: A private on-device weekly calorie ledger with manually entered meals, activity adjustment, a flexible remaining-range view, and optional symptom/energy note. Non-goals: food recognition, medical weight-loss plans, diagnosis, wearable sync, or social sharing.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 60% of participants log on at least 20 days and can explain their remaining weekly range without consulting a separate spreadsheet.
monetization: one-time — the core promise is no account, no ads, and a useful tool that remains usable offline.
constraints: Avoid eating-disorder-triggering language and medical claims; support an optional hidden-number mode; do not infer calorie expenditure from health data without explicit user input.
why_distinct: It is a flexible weekly planning ledger with personal context, not an AI nutrition coach or crowdsourced food database clone.

title: Low-Energy Menu
user: A household meal planner who needs a realistic weekly dinner plan that respects school meals, repeat fatigue, leftovers, and the cook's energy on each day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A commenter asks whether the meal-planning app actually limits recipes to locally in-stock food and challenges it to be more than an LLM funnel into Instacart or Kroger.
The household planner already models school-lunch repetition and the cook's daily energy budget, but the live planning path silently ignores both inputs.

recurrence: Two separate meal-planning discussions show that a weekly menu fails when it ignores real household context; the consequence is discarded plans and delivery-driven workarounds.
current_workaround: A paper week grid, recipe bookmarks, a generic meal-plan app, then last-minute takeout or manual substitutions.
incumbents_and_gap: Paprika, Plan to Eat, Mealime, and grocery-delivery meal planners organize recipes but typically optimize selection or shopping, not daily effort, school-food duplication, and leftover carryover together.
smallest_useful_product: An offline week grid where recipes carry effort, leftovers, and tags; users enter school/canteen meals and get a simple conflict/repetition warning plus a grocery export. Non-goals: recipe generation, grocery ordering, nutrition advice, or a recipe social network.
success_measure: Pilot households cook from the plan on at least four nights per week for three consecutive weeks and mark fewer than one planned dinner per week as abandoned for effort mismatch.
monetization: one-time — household planning data is personal and a compact offline utility can be bought outright.
constraints: No scraped recipe corpus; import only user-provided recipe data; make allergens and dietary tags user-entered rather than health claims.
why_distinct: The decision aid is effort and household context, not generated recipes or a grocery-delivery conversion funnel.

title: Recipe Source Card
user: A home cook saving web recipes who needs a clean, editable, source-attributed card without retyping ingredients or trusting a black-box scrape.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The recipe-app launch receives 74 comments, including reports that a common search such as 'Anti-inflammatory' crashes the app, showing how brittle broad recipe products can become.
The user story asks to paste a recipe URL, parse schema.org Recipe JSON-LD, map ingredients where possible, and open a pre-filled edit screen so recipes do not need retyping.

recurrence: A large recipe-app discussion and a separate 2026 feature request both point to capture reliability and editability as the real repeated task.
current_workaround: Browser bookmarks, screenshots, copy/paste into Notes, or importing into an opaque recipe app and correcting it by hand.
incumbents_and_gap: Paprika, Mela, Tandoor, and Mealie import recipes, but import failures and hidden transforms make provenance and repair difficult. The gap is a small capture tool that keeps the source, parsed fields, and user edits visible together.
smallest_useful_product: A local browser extension that extracts Recipe JSON-LD, preserves the canonical URL and attribution, shows a field-by-field editable preview, and exports JSON/Markdown. Non-goals: copying full sites without permission, a hosted recipe catalog, paywall bypassing, or AI rewriting.
success_measure: At least 85% of pilot imports create a usable card after fewer than three field edits, and every exported card retains its source URL.
monetization: one-time — source-preserving personal capture is a durable local utility with no server operating cost.
constraints: Respect site terms and robots boundaries; import only structured metadata exposed to the user; retain attribution and URL; do not redistribute copyrighted recipe text as a shared corpus.
why_distinct: It is a transparent, repairable personal capture pipeline, not a recipe database or thin LLM summarizer.

title: Glance Cart
user: A shopper moving through a store who needs a grocery list that stays visible and can be advanced with almost no unlock-and-reopen friction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker is investigating reliable extraction of actions from voice transcripts, specifically creating tasks, subtasks, and completing them, after seeing Todoist's voice-ramble flow.
The requester describes repeatedly unlocking, opening, and accidentally exiting a list for every item and asks for lock-screen visibility or raise-to-wake behavior.

recurrence: Two independent task-capture/use discussions in late 2025 and 2026; the in-store interaction cost repeats for every item in a trip.
current_workaround: A notes app, paper list, voice assistant, or a conventional grocery app that requires opening it for each checkoff.
incumbents_and_gap: AnyList, Bring!, Apple Reminders, and Google Keep handle lists and sharing; their primary interaction still assumes opening the app. The missing slice is a glanceable, aisle-oriented store mode.
smallest_useful_product: An Android app with a lock-screen/home-screen widget, large one-tap item advance, optional local speech-to-text capture, aisle groups, and QR export for a partner. Non-goals: grocery delivery, price comparison, advertising, account-based social lists, or LLM task parsing.
success_measure: In a timed 20-item shopping simulation, users mark 90% of items without opening the full app and finish at least 30% faster than with a standard notes list.
monetization: one-time — the value is a native convenience feature with no server required.
constraints: Lock-screen controls must comply with Android widget/notification rules; speech must remain on-device where available; do not expose shared-list content on a locked screen without user opt-in.
why_distinct: It is a store-mode interaction layer, not a broad grocery, delivery, or voice-assistant clone.

title: Fair Turn
user: Adults sharing a home who need recurring chores to rotate fairly, account for absences, and make swaps explicit without gamifying or surveilling each other.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN directly solicits people's best household-chore practices; replies span paying children, hiring help, and manual cleaning routines rather than a reliable shared system.
The feature request specifies automatic round-robin assignment, vacation skipping, and manual override so household members do not have to remember whose turn it is.

recurrence: Separate household-management requests across 2025–2026; recurring chores create interpersonal friction when turn-taking is remembered informally.
current_workaround: A paper chart, verbal reminders, recurring calendar events, a shared spreadsheet, or doing the task when someone notices it.
incumbents_and_gap: Tody, Sweepy, Nipto, and family chore apps emphasize gamification or parent-child rewards. Adult households need an auditable rotation and graceful absence/swap handling instead.
smallest_useful_product: An offline household PWA that defines chores, cadence, eligible people, vacation dates, equitable rotation, and a QR-shareable current board. Non-goals: points, parental controls, social feeds, contractor booking, or invasive reminders.
success_measure: After eight weeks, pilot households have at least 90% of recurring tasks assigned by the rotation and fewer than one unresolved 'whose turn?' dispute per month.
monetization: one-time — a household should own a small coordination utility without per-person subscriptions.
constraints: Use local-first sharing with explicit export/import; avoid collecting household relationship data; allow deletions and neutral language to reduce coercive-use risk.
why_distinct: It is fair rotation and exception handling for adults, not a gamified chores chart.

title: House History Pack
user: A homeowner who needs one durable history of appliances, seasonal work, repairs, warranties, permits, and contractor notes that can be handed to a buyer or service person.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The HN prompt asks what personal chore people automated, what they did manually before, and whether the automation remains dependable, highlighting continuing home-admin repetition.
A home-maintenance user requests an exportable PDF report and specifically wants permit documents included.

recurrence: Two 2026 discussions identify repeated personal administration and an explicit need to export home-maintenance evidence; losing history has financial and resale consequences.
current_workaround: Folders of receipts/manuals, email search, a calendar reminder, a spreadsheet, or starting a new note for every repair.
incumbents_and_gap: HomeZada, Centriq, and HomeBinder offer broad home platforms, often with accounts, marketplaces, or cloud lock-in. The gap is a local property record whose portable report is the primary artifact.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA for assets, service events, next-due tasks, warranty expiry, attached local files, and a selectable PDF/ZIP house-history pack. Non-goals: contractor marketplace, home valuation, smart-home control, or automated legal compliance advice.
success_measure: In a six-month pilot, 70% of users record at least five assets and can generate a complete maintenance packet for a chosen appliance in under two minutes.
monetization: one-time — a property record must remain accessible for years without a subscription lapse.
constraints: Files may contain addresses, invoices, and permits, so store locally by default and provide encrypted export; make report templates jurisdiction-neutral; respect document copyright.
why_distinct: The core deliverable is a portable proof/history pack, not a generic task reminder app.

title: Receipt to Room
user: A renter or homeowner returning from a large purchase who needs to turn receipts into a searchable room-level inventory for warranties, insurance, and household replenishment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants to export their own Amazon order history for tax paperwork and household management but cannot find an official route.
The feature request says manual/barcode entry is tedious after a large shopping trip and proposes receipt OCR bulk intake after comparing Sortly and HomeZada.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 requests focus on personal purchase history and bulk inventory intake; manual data entry is the adoption bottleneck.
current_workaround: Keep paper/email receipts, take photos, enter a few valuables manually in Sortly/HomeZada, or reconstruct purchases after a loss.
incumbents_and_gap: Sortly and HomeZada offer inventory systems and AI/photo features, but they are account-centric and optimize cataloging over transparent local receipt-to-room review. Amazon order export is not a household-inventory workflow.
smallest_useful_product: A local desktop app that OCRs user-selected receipt images, shows confidence-highlighted editable line items, assigns room/category/warranty date, and exports insurance-ready CSV/PDF. Non-goals: automatic retailer scraping, cloud receipt storage, valuation estimates, or filing claims.
success_measure: In pilot use, 75% of receipt lines are accepted or corrected in under 30 seconds per receipt and users can export a room inventory without retyping it.
monetization: one-time — local OCR and permanent household records have a clear owned-software value.
constraints: Receipts expose addresses and payment fragments; run OCR locally where possible, redact payment data on export, and clearly label OCR confidence; do not imply insurance coverage or valuation accuracy.
why_distinct: It makes receipt intake reviewable and local, instead of being a cloud home-inventory clone or retailer scraper.

title: Month Ahead Cash
user: A privacy-conscious household that needs to see whether manually entered cash, bills, and known irregular expenses will cover the next 30–60 days without linking a bank account.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A commenter on the long-maintained iOS budget app specifically praises its offline capability and later sync, saying more apps should use that model.
Actual Budget opened a consolidated feedback issue for its Budget Analysis report, evidence that making budget information legible remains active product work even in a mature local-first tool.

recurrence: Two current budgeting-product discussions show continuing demand for legible, offline financial views; the acute household question is cash timing, not a full accounting system.
current_workaround: A spreadsheet, calendar reminders, a notes list of bills, or a full budget product with manual or bank-linked transactions.
incumbents_and_gap: YNAB, Monarch, Copilot, Actual Budget, and spreadsheets are capable, but many users only need a fast, private answer to 'will the known bills clear?' without categories, imports, or financial-data aggregation.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA with opening cash, dated income/bills, optional sinking-fund envelopes, a daily projected balance line, and a printable month-ahead card. Non-goals: bank sync, investment tracking, credit advice, tax filing, or multi-user financial accounts.
success_measure: In a two-month pilot, users enter 90% of known bills before their due dates and correctly predict the lowest projected cash day within a 10% margin.
monetization: one-time — no-bank-linking, local ownership, and a narrow planning job support a paid utility rather than a subscription.
constraints: Financial data remains local by default; clearly distinguish forecasts from bank balances; protect exports with a passphrase option; never provide credit, investment, or tax advice.
why_distinct: It is a dated cash-survival view, not another zero-based-budget system or bank-data dashboard.

title: Bench Bin BOM
user: A home maker or small homelab builder who needs to compare a project bill of materials with parts already in drawers before ordering or starting a build.

evidence.quote_or_summary: DIY tool-sharing commenters say ease of listing is a primary barrier and describe buying general tools but borrowing friends' tools for one-off jobs.
The builder has no record of on-hand parts, repeatedly reorders an already-owned ESP32 or discovers a missing reed switch mid-build, and wants BOM shortages checked against real stock.

recurrence: Two independent DIY/maker discussions identify discovery and on-hand-stock uncertainty; it causes duplicate spending and mid-project interruption.
current_workaround: Memory, drawer labels, a spreadsheet, photos, a generic inventory package, or buying another part 'just in case.'
incumbents_and_gap: PartKeepr, InvenTree, and Homebox are flexible inventory systems; they are heavier than a personal bench workflow and do not make a simple project-BOM shortage card the main interaction.
smallest_useful_product: A local desktop app with bin locations, part photo/value/quantity, CSV BOM paste, shortage and substitute notes, and a print-friendly project pull list. Non-goals: supplier marketplace, barcode hardware requirement, team ERP, automatic purchasing, or agent control of tools.
success_measure: For ten planned builds, a pilot maker identifies all shortages before starting at least eight times and reports no duplicate purchase of a recorded part.
monetization: one-time — offline bench data and a project-focused workflow suit owned desktop software.
constraints: No proprietary distributor catalog scraping; import/export plain CSV; store photos locally; document that electrical substitutions require user review and are not safety advice.
why_distinct: The primary object is a build-ready BOM versus drawer stock, not a general warehouse system or tool-rental network.
